tier_reason: First-party benchstat tables in the README Performance section compare go-re2 against Go stdlib regexp and a cgo RE2 build; the harness is public (go run ./build bench-all in .github/workflows/bench.yaml, wafbench plus the stdlib regexp microbenchmarks), but the Go version and CPU model are not stated and the numbers come from one CI run, so C, not A.

corrections.workload: Go stdlib regexp microbenchmarks (Find, Compile, Match, MatchParallel at 16 B to 32 MB inputs) and wafbench (OWASP CoreRuleSet on Coraza: the FTW suite plus POST payloads of 1 B to 100 kB), run by the bench.yaml GitHub Actions workflow via go run ./build bench-all. The README tables were last updated on 2024-03-18 (PR #76) and were measured with the former wazero backend (the README then read 'accessed with the pure Go runtime, wazero'). They were not measured with the current default wasm2go translation: the default switched on 2026-07-08 (PR #251, a prose-only README change) and the wazero backend was retired on 2026-09-25 (PR #276).
corrections.claimed_speedup: wazero-backend build vs Go stdlib regexp (README, one CI run): WAF/POST/1000 15.399 ms vs 4.734 ms (-69.26%); POST/10000 150.65 ms vs 19.90 ms (-86.79%); POST/100000 1511.3 ms vs 171.7 ms (-88.64%); FTW 21.72 vs 21.17 (-2.55%); Match/Hard1/1M 214.239 ms vs 6.290 ms (about 34x, derived from page data); Match/Easy0i/1M 29,087,522 ns vs 42,975 ns (-99.85%, about 677x, derived from page data). The cgo (native RE2) build beats the wasm build by about 30% according to the README (POST/100000 110.4 ms vs 171.7 ms; Hard1/1M 1.895 ms vs 6.290 ms). Smaller inputs lose: Find 162.3 ns vs 1057.0 ns (+551%), Match/Easy0/16 3.721 ns vs 615.3 ns, POST/1 +18.18%, and compiles are about 4-6x slower (Compile/Onepass 4.017 us vs 23.585 us).
corrections.caveats: The README numbers date from March 2024 and the retired wazero backend. No published numbers exist for the current default wasm2go build, and the workflow artifacts behind each run are not in the README. Each table is one sample run on virtualised GitHub Actions hardware, with the Go version and CPU model unstated; the README itself says relative numbers within a run are only somewhat informative. Against the category's baseline (the same library compiled natively, i.e. the cgo RE2 column), the wasm build is slower: 1.56x on POST/100000 and 3.3x on Match/Hard1/1M (derived from page data). The largest Match wins (Easy0, Easy0i, Easy1, Medium, Hard: 99.8-99.9%) are $-anchored patterns. The cgo column stays at a constant ~155 ns from 16 B to 32 MB, so RE2 does not scan the input there (it matches from the end), and the wasm column's linear growth is mostly the cost of copying the input into wasm memory. Hard1 (an alternation of literals that needs a full scan) is the fairer large-input row, at about 34x. The library is slower than the stdlib for small inputs and simple expressions, and compiles are 4-6x slower. Behaviour differs from regexp on invalid UTF-8, and there is no *Reader support. Matching-semantics fixes landed after the measurement (#274 FindAll bytes, #275 POSIX and empty-match corner cases). It is a binding of RE2 (google/re2), which is already listed.

notes: Downgraded for misattribution, still tier C. The record presents the README numbers as the wasm2go build, but they were measured on the wazero backend, which was removed on 2026-09-25, so the current default build has no published numbers. Shortcomings to record: one CI sample with no Go version or CPU model; the wasm build is slower than the native cgo RE2 build (the category baseline); the headline Match wins come from $-anchored patterns that RE2 answers without scanning; it is slower on small inputs and 4-6x slower to compile. go-re2 is a Go binding of google/re2 (already listed, wave0-seed tier B), so the orchestrator may want to apply the wrapper/duplicate rule, although its claim (wasm packaging vs Go stdlib regexp) is distinct. Metadata checked: MIT, 210 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-29 (active).

tier_reason: The README's first-party Go benchmark table compares InkWasm with syscall/js, and the code is public (inkwasm/tests_js_test.go), but the browser, Go version and machine for the micro-benchmarks are not stated. The Gio frame-time table names the browsers and devices but is a rough '~' comparison of a fork against upstream. So C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Description: up to 2x faster than native syscall/js. ns/op for InkWasm generated bindings vs syscall/js: DOM 11,462 vs 23,550 (2.05x, derived from page data); SetLocalStorage 6,312 vs 11,796 (1.87x, derived); GetLocalStorage 3,300 vs 7,356 (2.23x, derived); GetLocationHostname 2,442 vs 1,979 (InkWasm 23% slower). With the InkWasm runtime API instead of generated bindings, DOM is 14,934 vs 23,550. The BytesRandom row (1,026 vs 1,808) is invalid and excluded (see caveats). Gio fork frame time, InkWasm fork vs upstream gioui.org@bed59024: about 3.02 ms vs 4.65 ms (Chrome 98, Ryzen 3900X), 20.03 vs 31.91 ms (Chrome 98, Xiaomi Note 9) and 4.84 vs 5.58 ms (Safari 15, MacBook Air), a 13% to 37% improvement per the README.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The README's 'Go 1.20+' line is the main branch's supported Go version, not the benchmark toolchain. The benchmark table is unchanged since tag v0.1.20 (the Go 1.18-1.20 line).
corrections.caveats: The BytesRandom benchmark is invalid. Its InkWasm side declares gen_GetRandom with //inkwasm:get globalThis.TestObject_GetRandom. For a get directive with one argument, the generator (parser/binder.go) emits a property lookup indexed by the byte slice (TestObject_GetRandom[slice]), so crypto.getRandomValues never runs and nothing is copied back. The syscall/js side invokes the function and calls CopyBytesToGo. The micro-benchmark environment (browser, Go version, hardware) is not stated, the numbers are one first-party run, and the table predates the May 2024 changes (Go 1.21+ compatibility #2, noescape and disabled verifications #5). One listed case (GetLocationHostname) is slower, and the README says results vary with how each API is used. The InkWasm DOM loop frees each object explicitly while syscall/js relies on finalizers. In the real Gio application the gain shrinks to 13-37%, measured on a fork against one upstream commit; the live comparison page (gio-bench.pages.dev) was not checked. The generator is experimental and rewrites source files in place. go:wasmexport is not supported.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim, still tier C: the BytesRandom row compares a property lookup that never calls the random function against a real call plus copy-back (wrong-work row; the other rows look equivalent). Shortcomings to record: invalid BytesRandom row; unstated micro-benchmark environment; one row slower; first-party, stale 2022-era numbers; only a 13-37% gain in the Gio app. Metadata checked: MIT, 38 stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-05-19 (stale).

tier_reason: First-party jest benchmark output in the README (code in __tests__/tests.spec.ts, describe('benchmarks')) compares the wasm build with jsclipper, the pure-JS port. The build flags are public (build/compile-asm.ts: em++ -O3), but the Emscripten version (unpinned emsdk Docker image) and the CPU ('my machine') are not stated, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: em++ -O3 --bind -s WASM=1 -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -s SINGLE_FILE=1 -s MODULARIZE=1 -s NO_FILESYSTEM=1 (build/compile-asm.ts), built in the unpinned emscripten/emsdk Docker image; the Emscripten version is not stated
corrections.claimed_speedup: From the README summary, relative to the pure-JS port (= 1.0): boolean ops on moderately big polygons about 0.4 for wasm (asm.js about 1.0); on small polygons about 0.7 for wasm (asm.js about 1.4); offsetting about 0.2 for wasm (asm.js about 0.5). Examples from the test output: 500 intersections of two 5000-point circles take 212 ms (wasm), 573 ms (pure JS) and 598 ms (asm.js); 100 miter offsets of a 5000-point circle with delta 5 take 129 ms (wasm) vs 702 ms (pure JS); 10000 intersections of two 100-point circles take 143 ms (wasm) vs 255 ms (pure JS).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from a single jest run on an unnamed machine under Node 17.9.0, not in a browser. Each mode runs once with no warmup, in the order wasm, asm.js, pure JS. The wasm timings include JS-to-wasm marshalling, which is fair as API cost. The pure-JS inputs are scaled up 100x (ScaleUpPaths) while the wasm inputs are not, and the offset deltas are not scaled, so the offset rows compare relatively different offsets; the boolean rows do identical work up to scale. The same library compiled natively, the category's first baseline, is not measured. The original C++ Clipper (polyclipping, Clipper1) is already listed, and this is its wasm build. The baseline jsclipper is not catalogued.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Tier C stands. Shortcomings to record: one unnamed machine; Node rather than a browser; no warmup or repetition; the native baseline is not measured; the pure-JS inputs are scaled 100x with unscaled offset deltas. The project is a wasm build of Clipper1, which is listed in wave 8 as https://sourceforge.net/projects/polyclipping (tier D), so the orchestrator may apply the wrapper/duplicate rule, although the wasm-vs-JS claim fits this category. Metadata checked: MIT, 176 stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-01-02 (stale); baseline_in_list corrected to false because jsclipper is not catalogued.
